extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in mathematical logic or computability theory
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter giving definitions, equivalent characterizations, closure properties, reducibility notions, classic undecidability results, Rice's theorem, and the fixed-point (recursion) theorem in computability theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computably enumerable set (Definition 149A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is computably enumerable (c.e.) if it is empty or the range of a computable function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: if S is the range of a computable function f then S = {f(0), f(1), f(2), ...} so f 'enumerates' S. Enumerations need not be increasing or injective (repetitions allowed); e.g., the constant function f(x)=0 enumerates {0}. Any computable (decidable) set is c.e. (construct f using the characteristic function χS). The c.e. notion is often called 'recursively enumerable' or 'semi-decidable' (you eventually get 'yes' for members, but may never get 'no' for non-members).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of c.e. sets (Theorem 1410A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S ⊆ N, the following are equivalent: (1) S is computably enumerable. (2) S is the range of a partial computable function. (3) S is empty or the range of a primitive recursive function. (4) S is the domain of a partial computable function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Kleene normal form and the universal T/U and predicate T(e,x,s) machinery to move between these forms. Clause (4) yields the common view S = {x : φ_e(x) ↓}, explaining why c.e. sets are 'sets of halting inputs'. These equivalences justify many interchangeable proof techniques: enumerate-by-range, enumerate-by-domain (halting inputs), or present as existentially quantified computable relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential relation characterization of c.e. sets (Theorem 1410B)
rubrics_metrics.description: S is computably enumerable iff there is a computable relation R(x,y) with S = {x : ∃y R(x,y)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the logical form ∃y R(x,y) for c.e. sets and yields a straightforward way to show c.e.: present a computable predicate R certifying membership. Conversely, from an enumeration you can build such an R. Often used to convert between formal logical statements and computability arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical c.e. sets: K0, K, K1 and existence of non-computable c.e. sets (Theorems 1411A, 1411B, Proposition 1417A)
rubrics_metrics.description: K0 = {⟨e,x⟩ : φ_e(x) ↓} (the halting set) and K = {e : φ_e(e) ↓} (the self-halting set) are c.e. but not computable. K1 = {e : φ_e(0) ↓} is c.e. but not computable. Every c.e. set equals W_e (the domain of φ_e) for some e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: enumerate halting computations to show c.e.; undecidability follows from the halting problem/self-reference diagonal arguments. These canonical sets are used as bases for reductions to prove undecidability of other sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure under union and intersection (Theorem 1412A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are computably enumerable then A ∪ B and A ∩ B are computably enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proofs provided: (i) from enumerating functions f and g for A and B, define h(x)=µy (f(y)=x ∨ g(y)=x) for A∪B and j similarly for A∩B by searching for matches in paired enumerations; (ii) interleaving enumeration k that alternates outputs of f and g enumerates A∪B; (iii) represent A and B as domains of partial functions m,n and note m + n has domain A∩B; (iv) simulate m and n in parallel to semi-decide union/intersection. Informally: to semi-decide membership in A∪B search both enumerations; for intersection search for x in both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-closure under complement and decidability criterion (Theorem 1413A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is computable iff both A and its complement A^c are computably enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: complements of c.e. sets need not be c.e. (otherwise every c.e. set would be computable). Apply to canonical sets to show certain complements are not c.e. (e.g., complement of K0 is not c.e.). Proof idea: if both are c.e. simulate enumerations for both and for any x one of them will produce a witness, giving a total computable decision procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-one reducibility (Definition 1414A) and basic properties (Propositions 1415A, 1415B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A computable function f is a many-one reduction of A to B (A ≤_m B) iff for all x, x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B. Many-one reducibility is transitive; if A ≤_m B and B is c.e./computable then A is c.e./computable respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use many-one reductions to show hardness: to prove A is at least as 'hard' as B give a computable transformation f. Composition of reductions yields transitivity. If B is c.e. and f reduces A to B then A is c.e. (pullback of domain). If B is decidable then A is decidable by composing χ_B with f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turing reducibility (discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turing reducibility allows a computable procedure to query an oracle for B while deciding A. It is a more liberal notion than many-one reducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key facts: if A is Turing reducible to B and B is computable then A is computable; unlike many-one reducibility, Turing reducibility does not require a single computable mapping and allows adaptively asking multiple queries. Complexity-theoretic analogues: Karp (many-one) and Cook (Turing) reducibilities with polynomial-time constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete computably enumerable sets (Definition 1416A and Theorem 1416B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A is complete c.e. (under many-one reducibility) if A is c.e. and every c.e. set B satisfies B ≤_m A. K, K0, and K1 are complete c.e. sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete c.e. sets are the 'hardest' c.e. problems; reductions from arbitrary c.e. sets to K0 (e.g., f(x)=⟨e,x⟩) show completeness. Use completeness to transfer undecidability: if a complete set were decidable then every c.e. set would be decidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of reductions to show noncomputability (§14.14 and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a set A is noncomputable (or non-c.e.), reduce a known hard set (e.g., K or K0) to A via a computable function f so that x ∈ known_set ⇔ f(x) ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reduce K0 to K1 by constructing ex that ignores its input and simulates e on x; use s-m-n and universal functions to produce indices implementing the simulation. Reductions can be many-one, one-one, Turing, etc., depending on context and required strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: s-m-n theorem and Kleene normal form as toolkit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Kleene's normal form theorem (universal function U and predicate T) and the s-m-n theorem to manipulate indices, fix parameters, and convert multi-ary computable functions to unary ones by 'hardwiring' inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications in proofs: write φ_e(x)=U(µs T(e,x,s)), construct primitive-recursive enumerators, obtain diag(x) giving index for φ_x(x,·), and produce functions s(e,x,y) with φ_{s(e,x,y)}(z) ≃ φ_{something}(x,y,z). These are essential for constructing self-referential programs, reductions, and fixed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rice's Theorem (Theorem 1419A) and undecidability of nontrivial index sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C be any class of partial computable functions and A = {n : φ_n ∈ C}. If A is decidable, then C is either empty or all partial computable functions. Equivalently, no nontrivial semantic property of computable functions (index set) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: syntactic/program questions can be decidable, but any nontrivial question about program behavior (e.g., 'is 17 in the range?', 'is φ_n total?', 'is φ_n constant?') is undecidable. Proof method: use fixed-point/self-reference and reduce the halting problem to membership in A. Corollaries list sample undecidable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point (recursion) theorem (Lemma 1420A, Theorem 1420B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every partial computable g(x,y) there exists an index e such that for all y, φ_e(y) ≃ g(e,y). Equivalent formulation: for every computable f(x) there is e with φ_e(y) ≃ φ_{f(e)}(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: you can construct programs that reference their own indices (self-referential programs), produce programs that print themselves, and perform diagonal constructions required in many undecidability proofs. Proof uses diag and s-m-n to produce e = diag(⌜l⌝) so φ_e(y) ≃ g(e,y). Also connects to fixed-point combinators in lambda calculus (Curry/Turing combinators). Useful for building functions defined in terms of their own index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tot (set of indices of total computable functions) undecidable (Proposition 1418A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tot = {x : φ_x is total (defined for all inputs)} is not computable (and in fact not c.e.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: reduce K to Tot by constructing a family of functions φ_{k(x)} that are total iff x ∈ K, using s-m-n. Intuition: if we could decide Tot, we could decide K. Note: Tot lies higher in the arithmetical hierarchy and is not even c.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerating c.e. sets via indices W_e (domains of φ_e)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each index e, define W_e = {x : φ_e(x) ↓}. Every c.e. set A equals W_e for some e (i.e., the W_e enumerate all c.e. sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification is used pervasively: to show a set is c.e. produce an e with W_e = A; to reduce to canonical sets use the mapping x ↦ ⟨e,x⟩ or s-m-n to produce indices whose domains capture desired behaviors. The W_e enumeration gives a convenient indexing of all c.e. sets for diagonal and completeness arguments.
